title: 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of elevated blood pressure and hypertension
authors: McEvoy JW, McCarthy CP, Bruno RM, Brouwers S, Canavan MD, Ceconi C, et al.; ESC Scientific Document Group
funder: Funding for the development of ESC Guidelines is derived entirely from the ESC with no involvement of the healthcare industry.
authorConflicts: All experts involved submitted declarations of interest; task force members with declared interests on specific topics were asked to abstain from voting on them. The individual declarations were not read.
result: Office blood pressure categories: non-elevated below 120/70 mm Hg; elevated 120 to 139 systolic or 70 to 89 diastolic; hypertension 140 or above systolic or 90 or above diastolic, unchanged as a definition. In elevated blood pressure, a 10-year predicted cardiovascular risk of 10% or more is considered sufficiently high to warrant lowering by lifestyle or drug treatment, with lifestyle measures for 3 months first and drugs recommended for confirmed pressure of 130/80 mm Hg or more; confirmed hypertension is recommended for treatment without further risk stratification. Adults receiving blood-pressure-lowering drugs should pursue a systolic target of 120 to 129 mm Hg if well tolerated, with more lenient targets for some patients and out-of-office confirmation. ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and diuretics are recommended as first-line options; beta-blockers can be added preferentially for angina, heart failure, after myocardial infarction or for heart-rate control, are less effective at preventing stroke, have a higher discontinuation rate due to side effects, are associated with new-onset diabetes in predisposed patients, especially with diuretics, and should be avoided in isolated systolic hypertension or arterial stiffness; in resistant hypertension a beta-blocker, preferably vasodilating, is an alternative to a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist as fourth-line treatment.
